title: Pawn Chase!
summary: Keep both minor pieces, then stop a pawn race by threatening mate instead of chasing promotion squares.

nodes.question: Can White stop the connected pawns and still win?
nodes.explanation: The bishop and knight must both survive if White is to force a win. A direct blockade can stop the pawns while losing the knight.

nodes.question: How does Bd4 attack more than a pawn?
nodes.explanation: The bishop can attack b2 while threatening Bf6 mate. The king and knight already cover the black king’s escape squares.

branches.title: Preserve the knight and threaten mate
commentary: Begin from the complete six-piece source board. Follow the illustrated ...Ke8 defense against the bishop check.
Bc5+ checks Kf8 along the diagonal while preparing Ba3 against less active king retreats.
Ke8 attacks Nd8, trying to force White to waste a tempo saving the knight.
Nb7 saves that knight and prepares to check from d6.
b2 advances the dangerous passer, apparently threatening promotion before the knight can stop it.
Nd6+ checks and coordinates with Bc5. Black must answer the check before promoting.
Kd8 avoids the bishop’s discovered-check lines and keeps the promotion threat.
Bd4 attacks b2 along the diagonal and threatens Bf6 mate, turning the race into a double threat.
b1=Q promotes, but the new queen does not defend the black king’s mating cage.
Bf6# is actual mate. Nd6 covers c8 and e8, Kc6 covers c7 and d7, and the bishop checks along f6–e7–d8.
branches.explanation: Bf6# is actual mate. Nd6 covers c8 and e8, Kc6 covers c7 and d7, and the bishop checks along f6–e7–d8.

branches.title: Defend the passer instead of promoting
commentary: Compare the source’s alternative of supporting the b-pawn.
Bd4 combines an attack on b2 with the mating threat on f6.
a3 protects b2, but leaves the black king’s escape squares unchanged.
Bf6# is still actual mate. Defending the attacked pawn does not answer the more urgent threat.
branches.explanation: Bf6# is still actual mate. Defending the attacked pawn does not answer the more urgent threat.

branches.title: Block the pawns before saving the knight
commentary: Compare the source’s first tempting blockade.
Bd4 aims at b2 immediately, but gives up the forced win.
a3 supports the b-pawn’s advance and makes a simple permanent blockade impossible.
Bc5+ gains time to capture a3, but cannot also save Nd8.
Ke8 attacks the knight while answering the bishop check.
Bxa3 removes the a-pawn and aims to stop the remaining passer.
Kxd8 removes the knight. The exact bishop-versus-pawn ending is drawn; stopping promotion alone has not preserved winning material.
branches.explanation: Kxd8 removes the knight. The exact bishop-versus-pawn ending is drawn; stopping promotion alone has not preserved winning material.

exercises.prompt: Why can Black not simply promote after Bd4?
exercises.answer: Bf6 is mate. The knight and white king cover the escape squares, and the newly promoted queen on b1 cannot answer that check.

exercises.prompt: Why is stopping the pawns not enough?
exercises.answer: The early bishop blockade loses Nd8. The remaining bishop can hold the pawn but cannot force mate against the lone king once the pawn is gone.

startContext: The complete six-piece source board and selected ...Ke8/...Kd8 route are reconstructed from saved images. Both illustrated defenses to Bd4 lead to actual Bf6 mate. The early blockade is checked as a draw. Other king retreats and discovered-check branches remain source context; no exhaustive tree is claimed.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
